depth.summary: Euthanasia must minimise pain, distress and anxiety before loss of consciousness, and failure of that standard is named dysthanasia. Death must be confirmed before disposal using a combination of absent pulse, breathing, corneal reflex and pain response, no audible heartbeat, gray mucous membranes and eventually rigor mortis, with no single sign except rigor mortis sufficient; the AVMA guidance warns that deeply narcotised animals may appear dead and recover, and ectothermic species require a longer assessment or an adjunctive method. Disposal must be legal and must prevent contamination, animals intended for food must not receive a barbiturate, and scavenger risk applies to buried remains. Owners and staff may both be distressed, which makes communication and debrief part of the procedure. The technician prepares, supports, assists confirmation, cares for the body and documents; the method, the drugs and the confirmation are veterinary.

readings.title: Merck Veterinary Manual, Euthanasia of Animals
readings.note: Read the criteria for a good death, acceptable techniques, confirmation of death, disposal of remains and the section on psychological well-being of human participants. The chapter defines euthanasia as ending life while minimising pain, distress and anxiety before loss of consciousness, defines dysthanasia, lists the combined criteria for confirming death and states that none alone except rigor mortis is sufficient, notes that adjunctive methods may be needed in ectothermic animals whose heartbeat and respiration are difficult to assess, requires legal disposal that prevents contamination, and states that animals intended for food should not be euthanased with a barbiturate. It is peer reviewed and dated, and is the primary source for this lesson.

readings.title: Merck Veterinary Manual, Agents and Methods of Euthanasia by Species (table)
readings.note: Read the rows for dogs, cats, rabbits, birds, reptiles and fish. The table distinguishes acceptable methods from acceptable methods with conditions, and shows that intravenous barbiturates are acceptable for dogs, cats, rabbits and birds, while reptiles, amphibians and fish require species-appropriate agents and often an adjunctive method. It is adapted from the AVMA guidelines, so it is a summary rather than the full standard; use it to understand that method selection is species-specific and veterinary, not to select an agent.

readings.title: Iowa State University, Secondary Steps and Confirmation of Death (veterinary teaching page)
readings.note: Read the confirmation of death section. It gives a step-by-step assessment: check for a heartbeat with a stethoscope placed just behind the left elbow rather than relying on a pulse, observe respiration with the caveat that breathing may be irregular or absent in an unconscious animal, test the corneal reflex, and confirm over time, with at least five minutes of absent heartbeat, respiration and corneal reflex, and consultation with a supervisor when in doubt. This is a university teaching page for production animal and laboratory contexts, so the intervals are conservative; that conservatism is the reason it is cited here for small or difficult to assess patients.

visual.title: Euthanasia sequence with confirmation gate
visual.description: A text-based timeline of the procedure from consent to aftercare, with a confirmation gate that cannot be passed on a single sign.
steps: Stage 1, before: confirm identity and consent, discuss the sequence and the possibility of catheter placement, offer pre-euthanasia sedation as the veterinarian decides, and prepare a quiet space and the equipment.
Stage 2, access and sedation: place intravenous access where appropriate, record the drugs and route, and allow the sedation to take effect before positioning.
Stage 3, the procedure: the veterinarian administers the euthanasia solution while the technician restrains gently, narrates for the owner and observes the patient.

Confirmation gate: absent heartbeat on auscultation behind the left elbow, absent breathing observed for at least five minutes, absent corneal reflex, absent response to a firm toe pinch, gray mucous membranes; rigor mortis as a later supporting sign. No single sign passes the gate.

Stage 4, after: allow the owner time, shroud and identify the body, explain storage and the lawful disposal options, warn about barbiturate residue and scavenger risk, and offer the owner a follow-up contact.
Stage 5, staff: a short debrief and a log entry, because the procedure affects the people who perform it.

questions.prompt: A fictional 4 kg cat with hepatic lipidosis has eaten nothing for nine days. The veterinarian orders enteral feeding. The technician is asked to describe the first day's plan. Which plan matches the evidence in this level?
questions.answer: Begin at about one third of the resting energy requirement over the first 12 to 24 hours, reassess tolerance, and increase gradually toward the full requirement over two to three days while monitoring phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
questions.distractor: Begin at the full resting energy requirement immediately, because the deficit has accumulated for nine days and must be corrected quickly.
questions.correction: Refeeding syndrome is the risk that reverses the intuition. In the feline case material, hypophosphataemia appeared 12 to 72 hours after feeding began in chronically malnourished cats, and the ISFM guidelines describe the syndrome as a reason to cease feeding and restart below the calculated requirement. The distractor corrects a nine-day deficit in one day and would produce the electrolyte shift the lesson warns about. Volumes and the feeding plan remain veterinary decisions; the technician measures intake and reports intolerance.

questions.prompt: A fictional 5 kg cat has had an indwelling urinary catheter for three days after relief of urethral obstruction. The overnight nurse reports 4 mL of urine in the last hour and a catheter that has been disconnected twice for flushing. Which response is most appropriate?
questions.answer: Treat the low volume and the disconnections as two separate reportable problems: record the hourly volume against the expected 1 to 2 mL/kg/h, note each disconnection, and escalate both to the veterinarian because oliguria and breaks in the closed system carry different risks.
questions.distractor: Flush the catheter again and wait until the morning, since a blocked catheter is the most likely explanation and flushing solves it.
questions.correction: Four millilitres in an hour in a 5 kg cat is 0.8 mL/kg/h, below the 1 to 2 mL/kg/h range that Merck's critical care chapter gives as normal, and the cause might be obstruction, dehydration, or post-obstructive physiology rather than a simple plug. Flushing is a procedure with its own risk of introducing infection and of overdistending the bladder, and repeated disconnection defeats the closed system whose value the randomised trial in lesson 87 supports. The correct move is measurement, documentation and escalation.

questions.prompt: A fictional 28 kg dog has been recumbent for two days after spinal surgery. The ward is short-staffed and the turn chart has entries at 08:00 and 20:00. The technician notices a non-blanching red area over the left greater trochanter. What is the best interpretation and action?
questions.answer: Twelve-hourly turning is below the two-hourly repositioning described in the rehabilitation literature, the non-blanching area is early pressure injury rather than a cosmetic mark, so the technician should start a documented turn schedule, add pressure relief and escalate the skin finding.
questions.distractor: The red area is expected in a recumbent dog and will resolve once the patient walks again, so it should be left undisturbed to avoid further skin damage.
questions.correction: Stage one pressure injury is defined by intact skin with blanching or non-blanching erythema, warmth and induration, and it is reversible with care, which is exactly why it must be reported at this point. Leaving the area undisturbed is the opposite of treatment: the injury is caused by unrelieved pressure over a bony prominence, so relief is the intervention. The turn interval matters more than the chart's tidiness, and a two-hourly schedule is the working standard in the sources for this lesson.

questions.prompt: A fictional client is being discharged with a diabetic cat and a new insulin pen. At the end of the appointment the technician says, 'Any questions?' and the client says no. Two weeks later the cat is hypoglycaemic and the record shows the client was using the wrong syringe scale. Which change to the discharge process would most likely have prevented this?
questions.answer: Use a return demonstration with the client's own device, checking the syringe scale against the pen, and document what the client did rather than what the client said.
questions.distractor: Provide a longer written handout with the dose printed in bold, because the failure was one of information supply.
questions.correction: The failure was performance, not information. Teach-back is defined as explaining something and then asking the recipient to explain or show it back, and the systematic reviews in lesson 89 report improved knowledge and skill when the check is built into the encounter. A handout cannot reveal that the client has picked up a U-100 syringe for a U-40 product, whereas a return demonstration can. Documentation should record the demonstration, not the absence of questions.

questions.prompt: A fictional 14-year-old dog with end-stage renal disease is euthanased in the practice. Ten minutes after the injection the veterinarian is called away, and the technician is asked to confirm death before the body is placed in the freezer. Which confirmation is adequate?
questions.answer: A combination of absent pulse, absent breathing, absent corneal reflex, no response to a firm toe pinch, no audible heartbeat on auscultation and grey mucous membranes, documented as a set, because no single sign except rigor mortis is sufficient.
questions.distractor: Absence of a palpable femoral pulse for one minute is sufficient, because circulation stops before respiration in every species.
questions.correction: Merck's euthanasia chapter states that a combination of criteria is most reliable and that none of the signs alone, except rigor mortis, confirms death. The distractor selects one sign and adds a physiological claim that is not true across species; in ectothermic patients, for example, heartbeat and respiration are described as difficult to assess, which is why adjunctive methods are used. Confirmation and documentation belong to the veterinarian, and the technician's role is to support the assessment and record it accurately.

questions.prompt: A fictional 7 kg cat with a urethral obstruction arrives with a potassium of 8.1 mEq/L and a heart rate of 90 beats per minute with poor pulse quality. The technician connects the ECG, places the patient on oxygen and prepares the catheter trolley. Explain what the ECG is being used to detect, why the potassium result needs a handling check before it is treated as real, and who decides the interventions.
questions.answer: The ECG is there to detect the conduction consequences of hyperkalaemia, namely bradycardia, tall T waves, widening of the QRS complex, loss of P waves and progression toward a sine wave pattern. The handling check covers pseudohyperkalaemia from thrombocytosis, extreme leukocytosis, haemolysis in breeds such as the Akita and Shiba Inu, EDTA contamination and delayed serum separation. Relief of obstruction and any electrolyte or fluid intervention are veterinarian decisions, with the technician monitoring, documenting and escalating.
questions.distractor: The ECG is there to confirm the potassium result, and because the value is above 7 mEq/L the technician should start the potassium-lowering fluidbag that is kept prepared in the crash cart.
questions.correction: The ECG shows the effect of potassium on the myocardium, not the concentration itself, and a normal trace does not make a high result artefact-free or harmless. The distractor also crosses the scope boundary by initiating treatment. Lesson 84 separates measurement, interpretation and prescription; lesson 87 covers the obstruction that usually explains this presentation. The correct answer keeps the three roles distinct and names the sample-handling traps that change what the number means.

questions.prompt: A fictional 22 kg dog with a perforated intestine is four hours post-operative. Blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg with a mean of 52 mm Hg, lactate is 4.6 mmol/L, urine output is 0.3 mL/kg/h, and the dog is quiet but responsive. A colleague describes the patient as 'stable because the temperature is normal'. Build the argument that corrects this description, using the sepsis consensus material.
questions.answer: Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening syndrome from a dysregulated host response to infection that produces organ dysfunction, and septic shock is the subset with cardiovascular instability and metabolic abnormalities despite adequate fluid resuscitation. This patient has hypotension below the mean arterial target of 60 mm Hg, hyperlactataemia and oliguria, which are organ dysfunction, so the correct description is a patient with sepsis and possible septic shock who needs urgent veterinary assessment, not a stable patient.
questions.distractor: The patient is stable because a normal temperature excludes sepsis, and the low blood pressure is expected after anaesthesia.
questions.correction: Normal temperature does not exclude sepsis, and the consensus work explicitly moved away from SIRS criteria, which include temperature, as the basis for diagnosis. The distractor uses one normal parameter to overrule three abnormal ones. Lesson 82 requires organ dysfunction to be identified and a structured severity assessment to be used, and lesson 43 established that perfusion is read from a set of observations rather than a single value.

questions.prompt: A fictional practice measures blood pressure in every cat over nine years of age using an oscillometric device, one measurement, with the cuff on the tail while the cat is held in lateral recumbency by two people. A 12-year-old cat reads 185 mm Hg systolic and the veterinarian is asked to start treatment. Identify the three protocol failures and state what the ACVIM statement requires before a diagnosis.
questions.answer: The failures are single rather than repeated measurement, a device and site used without regard to validation and standard technique, and restraint and posture that generate situational hypertension. The statement requires reliable measurement with a standard protocol, ideally by an experienced operator, and confirmation on more than two occasions unless target organ damage is present; a reading of 180 mm Hg or more without target organ damage is still not a diagnosis on one occasion.
questions.distractor: The only failure is using the tail rather than a forelimb, and a single reading above 180 mm Hg is sufficient to treat because the risk category is severe.
questions.correction: Site matters, but the larger failures are repetition, technique and the stress of restraint, which the statement names as situational hypertension. The distractor treats the severity band as a diagnosis, when the band describes risk once hypertension is established. Lesson 83's decision rule is that the number is the output of a protocol, and lesson 65 established that handling is a physiological variable, not a convenience.

questions.prompt: A fictional 3.6 kg cat with a newly diagnosed diabetic crisis has a blood glucose of 486 mg/dL, venous pH 7.21, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.8 mmol/L and potassium 3.2 mEq/L. The veterinarian starts an insulin infusion. List the four variables the technician should be measuring, with the interval and the reason for each.
questions.answer: Blood glucose every one to two hours because the infusion is titrated to it and the fall should not exceed 50 to 100 mg/dL per hour; potassium every four to six hours initially because insulin drives potassium into cells and total body potassium is already depleted; venous pH or bicarbonate to track resolution of acidosis toward a pH above 7.35; and urine output plus hydration and mentation to track the osmotic diuresis and the response to fluids.
questions.distractor: Blood glucose every six hours is sufficient, and potassium can wait for the next day because a low value will correct itself once insulin is running.
questions.correction: Six-hourly glucose cannot detect the rate of fall that matters, and potassium does the opposite of correcting itself: insulin shifts potassium intracellularly, so a patient at 3.2 mEq/L is at risk of a further fall and arrhythmia. The distractor reverses the physiology. Lesson 85's rule is that the monitoring interval is set by the half-life of the risk, not by the shift pattern, and that insulin and fluid prescriptions belong to the veterinarian.

questions.prompt: A fictional 6 kg cat with pancreatitis has not eaten for four days and vomits when fed by mouth. Compare a naso-oesophageal tube with an oesophagostomy tube for this patient, naming one advantage, one contraindication and one daily maintenance task for each, and state the caloric starting point.
questions.answer: A naso-oesophageal tube needs no general anaesthesia and suits short-term use of roughly three to five days, but it is contraindicated in a patient that is vomiting and requires liquid diets, with daily checks of position, fixation and nasal comfort. An oesophagostomy tube needs anaesthesia and is suited to longer use with blended diets, is also contraindicated while vomiting is uncontrolled, and requires daily stoma cleaning, a light dressing and flushing after every feed. Feeding starts at about one third of the resting energy requirement over the first 12 to 24 hours.
questions.distractor: Both tubes are equivalent, so the choice should be made on cost alone, and feeding should start at the full resting energy requirement because the patient has a four-day deficit.
questions.correction: The tubes differ in placement, duration, diet tolerance and complication profile, and the vomiting makes both routes unsafe until it is controlled, which is a shared contraindication rather than a difference. Starting at full requirement is the refeeding error described in lesson 86. The distractor answers a clinical question with a purchasing question and then adds the one arithmetic mistake that the feline refeeding literature warns against.

questions.prompt: A fictional 5 kg cat is admitted with a blocked urethra. The technician is asked to prepare the catheterisation trolley and the monitoring sheet. Describe the aseptic and system choices that matter, one piece of evidence about closed systems, and the two urine volumes that would make the technician escalate.
questions.answer: Use a sterile, soft indwelling catheter of appropriate French size, a strict aseptic placement protocol, secure fixation and a closed collection system that is not disconnected for convenience. The randomised trial in 51 dogs found nosocomial bacteriuria in 11.1 percent of open systems and 8.3 percent of closed systems, not significantly different, and concluded that a strict placement and maintenance protocol was likely the key factor. Escalate a urine output below about 0.5 mL/kg/h, and escalate the high output of post-obstructive diuresis, which can exceed the normal 1 to 2 mL/kg/h by a wide margin.
questions.distractor: The closed system is the only thing that matters, so the catheter can be disconnected for flushing as often as needed as long as the bag is sterile.
questions.correction: The trial's own conclusion refuses that inference: the low incidence in both groups was attributed to the strict protocol, not to the bag alone. Disconnecting for flushing breaks the system and adds a route for ascending infection. Lesson 87 places the technician's contribution in technique and measurement, and lesson 59 established the barrier logic that makes a closed system useful only while it stays closed.

questions.prompt: A fictional 30 kg dog is recumbent after a fibrocartilaginous embolus. It is incontinent of urine, cannot turn itself, and has a dry cornea on the dependent eye. Build a nursing plan with four timed elements and the physiological reason for each.
questions.answer: Reposition every two hours from left lateral to right lateral to sternal, because unrelieved pressure over the trochanter, ischium and scapula causes capillary occlusion and pressure injury; inspect and clean the skin at each turn, with moisture control because urine macerates skin; lubricate and check both eyes at least every four hours, because recumbency reduces blink and tear spread and the dependent cornea is exposed; and provide passive range of motion and sling or hoisting sessions, because immobility costs joint range, muscle mass and ventilation.
questions.distractor: Reposition every six hours and focus on keeping the patient clean, because skin hygiene is the only modifiable risk in recumbency.
questions.correction: Six-hourly repositioning leaves pressure unrelieved for long enough to produce injury in a large dog, and hygiene alone does not address pressure, shear or the respiratory consequences of a fixed position. The distractor also omits the eye, which is the most quickly damaged structure in a laterally recumbent patient. Lesson 88 treats the turn schedule as a prescription with a time, an observation and a record, not as an optional comfort measure.

questions.prompt: A fictional client must give subcutaneous fluids to a 4 kg cat at home twice weekly. The veterinarian has prescribed the volume. The technician has ten minutes at discharge. Design the teaching sequence and name two things that must be documented.
questions.answer: Explain the purpose in plain language, demonstrate the full sequence with the equipment the client will use, then ask the client to perform it while the technician observes and coaches, using teach-back rather than asking whether they understood. Document the demonstration, the client's performance and any part still uncertain, the equipment and needle size supplied, the prescribed volume and frequency as written by the veterinarian, and the follow-up contact plan.
questions.distractor: Give the client a printed sheet and ask them to watch a video at home, because ten minutes is not enough for a demonstration and adults learn best from written instructions.
questions.correction: The teach-back reviews report that knowledge and skill improve when the recipient explains or performs the task back, and that reinforcement after discharge matters for sustained benefit. A sheet and a video cannot show whether this client can hold a cat, find a site and attach the line. Lesson 89's rule is that discharge teaching ends with evidence of performance, not with the delivery of information, and the prescribed volume remains the veterinarian's decision.

questions.prompt: A fictional 11-year-old Labrador is euthanased at home. The owner asks whether the eyes will stay open, whether the body can be buried in the garden, and how the technician knows the dog has died. Answer all three, naming the limits of each answer.
questions.answer: The eyes may remain open and the cornea will dull, which is a normal post-mortem change and not evidence of suffering; burial is a legal and practical question that depends on local rules, depth, distance from water and whether the drug used leaves residue hazardous to scavengers, so the practice must give the owner the locally correct options; death is confirmed on a combination of absent pulse, breathing, corneal reflex and pain response, no audible heartbeat, grey mucous membranes and eventually rigor mortis, with confirmation belonging to the veterinarian.
questions.distractor: The eyes closing is the reliable sign of death, and burial is always acceptable because the drug is broken down within hours in soil.
questions.correction: Eye position is not a criterion of death at all, and the claim about barbiturate breakdown is both unsupported and unsafe, because residues can be hazardous to wildlife that scavenge a buried carcass. The distractor invents a sign and a reassurance. Lesson 90 requires the technician to know which questions can be answered, which must be referred, and which require a legal rather than a medical answer.

questions.prompt: A fictional 8 kg pug with brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome is recovering from anaesthesia. The technician must choose between flow-by oxygen, a facemask and a nasal line, and must state what would make each choice wrong. Construct the comparison.
questions.answer: Flow-by is the least invasive and delivers roughly 25 to 40 percent, useful while the patient is waking but easily displaced and dependent on the operator; a facemask reaches roughly 35 to 60 percent but is poorly tolerated in a dyspnoeic brachycephalic patient and risks carbon dioxide accumulation if too tight; a unilateral nasal line reaches roughly 30 to 50 percent with less handling but requires patience, fixation and humidification, and is wrong if the patient resents it or the nares are obstructed.
questions.distractor: Intubation is the correct answer whenever saturation is below 95 percent, because it delivers 100 percent oxygen and removes the airway problem.
questions.correction: Intubation delivers 100 percent but requires anaesthesia or a patient tolerant of a tube, and it does not remove the obstruction; it bypasses it while the patient is intubated and creates a new set of risks on extubation. The distractor reaches for the highest fraction and the most invasive route at the moment the patient needs the least handling. Lesson 81 and lesson 36 both treat oxygen delivery as a ladder chosen by effort, tolerance and the measured response.

questions.prompt: A fictional ward has one monitor, one oxygen cage and two critical patients: a 5 kg cat with sepsis and a 40 kg dog with pneumonia. The technician must allocate the equipment for the next hour and justify the choice using measured variables rather than diagnosis.
questions.answer: Allocate by the variable most likely to change management within the hour: the cat's small size makes blood pressure and urine output the most informative and most easily lost signals, and its sepsis makes perfusion the priority, so the monitor and a warmed, quiet cage go to the cat, while the dog receives oxygen by a technique that does not need the cage and a written observation set at fixed intervals. Both get a documented rationale and a review time, with escalation if either fails to improve.
questions.distractor: Give both resources to the dog, because a 40 kg patient has less physiological reserve than a 5 kg patient and larger patients deteriorate faster.
questions.correction: Body size is not a reserve measurement, and the claim reverses the actual arithmetic: smaller patients have smaller absolute circulating volumes and lose heat faster, and a 5 kg cat's urine output is measured in single millilitres per hour. The distractor uses size as a proxy for risk, which is exactly the reasoning error lesson 71 identified. The correct answer allocates by measured need, documents the decision and sets a review time.

questions.prompt: A fictional technician is asked to write the one-page standard for the practice's oxygen, blood pressure and feeding-tube checks. Write the four rules you would insist on, each with the error it prevents.
questions.answer: Record the delivered technique and flow with every saturation, because a number without its oxygen conditions cannot be trended; measure blood pressure with a standard protocol, repeated readings and minimal restraint, because single stressed readings create diagnoses; calculate and record actual calories delivered against the resting energy requirement, because a tube in place is not the same as nutrition delivered; and write the escalation threshold next to each variable, because a value without a trigger is an observation nobody acts on.
questions.distractor: Record the values in the same place each day and let the veterinarian interpret them at ward rounds, because standardisation of the form is what makes a monitoring system reliable.
